content: 1. When the certainty of evidence is low, our confidence in the estimated effect is limited. This means that the true effect may differ significantly from the estimated effect. 2. When the certainty of evidence is very low, we have minimal confidence in the estimated effect. The true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimated effect. 3. Evidence was downgraded by one level due to imprecision and inconsistency. The confidence intervals are wide, and the direction of the effect varies across the included studies. 4. Evidence was downgraded by one level due to indirectness. For example, one study contributing data was conducted among stunted, moderately anemic children aged 3–4 years living in a poor community on the outskirts of Lima, Peru, who were at high risk for zinc deficiency. 5. Evidence was downgraded by one level due to imprecision. The confidence interval is very broad, and the data comes from only one study conducted among stunted, moderately anemic children aged 3–4 years in a poor community on the outskirts of Lima, Peru, at high risk for zinc deficiency. 6. Evidence was downgraded by one level due to limitations in study design or execution, indicating a risk of bias. For instance, in one study, participants were divided into five groups based on the order in which they visited the hospital for antenatal care, without proper sequence generation. 7. The risk in the intervention group, along with its 95% confidence interval, is based on the assumed risk in the comparison group and the relative effect of the intervention, as well as its 95% confidence interval. 8. The GRADE Working Group defines high-certainty evidence as evidence where we are very confident that the true effect is close to the estimated effect. 9. Moderate-certainty evidence indicates that we are moderately confident in the estimated effect, but there is a possibility that the true effect may differ substantially. 10. Low-certainty evidence reflects limited confidence in the estimated effect, with the true effect potentially differing significantly. 11. Very low-certainty evidence indicates very little confidence in the estimated effect, with the true effect likely to differ substantially. 12. Evidence was downgraded by one level for indirectness and one level for imprecision. Wide confidence intervals suggest the possibility of either an increase or decrease in the outcome. The study was conducted among children aged 6–13 years from four schools in neighboring villages in St. Thomas, Batangas, approximately 60 km south of Manila, Philippines. 13. The outcomes of interest for wheat flour fortification with iron include iron status, iron deficiency, iron deficiency anemia, anemia, adverse effects (such as iron overload), dietary iron intake, cognitive and motor skill development in children, cognitive and work performance in adults, malaria incidence and severity, other infections (e.g., sepsis), and birth/pregnancy outcomes (e.g., birth weight, gestational age, maternal mortality). 14. The outcomes of interest for wheat flour fortification with folic acid include neural tube defects, other birth defects, folate status (measured by serum or red cell folate), cancer (any type or colorectal), adverse effects, vitamin B12 deficiency, dietary folate intake, serum homocysteine concentrations, anemia, drug efficacy (e.g., sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, cotrimoxazole), malaria incidence and severity, and birth/pregnancy outcomes (e.g., birth weight, gestational age, maternal mortality). 15. The outcomes of interest for wheat flour fortification with zinc include zinc status, stunting or wasting in children, dietary zinc intake, and other health outcomes related to zinc deficiency. 16. Subgroup analyses for wheat flour fortification interventions consider factors such as the type and amount of micronutrient added, population characteristics (e.g., age, nutritional status, risk of deficiency), and consumption patterns of wheat flour. 17. Control groups in these studies typically involve the same wheat flour without added micronutrients or no intervention at all. 18. The effectiveness of wheat flour fortification as a public health strategy is evaluated based on its impact on specific health outcomes, with evidence graded according to the GRADE Working Group criteria.
